question: To control a motorcycle well, you should sit far enough forward on the seat so that:
choice_a: Your arms are fully extended and straight
choice_b: You lean back against a sissy bar
choice_c: Your arms are slightly bent when you hold the handlegrips
choice_d: Your knees point outward away from the tank
explanation: Sit far enough forward so that your arms are slightly bent when you hold the handlegrips; bending your arms permits you to press on the handlebars without stretching.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.12, 'Body Position'

question: Why does the handbook recommend starting with your right wrist flat on the handgrip?
choice_a: It reduces vibration in cold weather
choice_b: It is a legal requirement for licensing
choice_d: It helps keep you from accidentally using too much throttle
explanation: Start with your right wrist flat -- this will help you keep from accidentally using too much throttle.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.12, 'Body Position'

question: While riding, your knees should be:
choice_a: Against the gas tank, to help you keep your balance as the motorcycle turns
choice_b: Pointed outward away from the motorcycle
explanation: Keep your knees against the gas tank to help you keep your balance as the motorcycle turns.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.12, 'Body Position'

question: According to the handbook, your feet should remain:
choice_b: Firmly on the footpegs, without dragging, to maintain balance and control
choice_c: Crossed over each other for stability
choice_d: Pointed downward toward the road surface
explanation: Keep your feet firmly on the footpegs to maintain balance; don't drag your feet, and don't let your toes point downward, since they may get caught between the road and the footpegs.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.12, 'Body Position'

question: While stopped in traffic, the handbook advises remaining in which gear so you can move out quickly if needed?
choice_d: Whatever gear you happened to be in before stopping
explanation: Shift down through the gears with the clutch as you slow or stop, and remain in first gear while stopped so you can move out quickly if you need to.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.12, 'Shifting Gears'

question: If you shift into a lower gear without slowing enough first, what can happen?
choice_a: The engine will automatically stall safely with no other effect
choice_b: Nothing; gear changes have no effect on motorcycle behavior
choice_c: The front tire will suddenly go flat
choice_d: The motorcycle may lurch and the rear wheel may skid
explanation: Make certain you are riding slowly enough when you shift into a lower gear -- if not, the motorcycle will lurch and the rear wheel may skid.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.12-13, 'Shifting Gears'

question: When downshifting, the handbook says riders should work toward:
choice_b: Releasing the clutch as abruptly as possible
choice_c: Shifting without using the clutch at all
choice_d: Holding the clutch fully engaged indefinitely
explanation: Work toward a smooth, even clutch release, especially when downshifting.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.13, 'Shifting Gears'

question: According to the handbook, it is generally best to shift gears:
choice_a: Only while in the middle of a turn
choice_b: Before entering a turn, rather than during it
choice_c: Only after fully completing a turn
choice_d: Timing of the shift makes no difference at all
explanation: It is best to change gears before entering a turn; however, if shifting in the turn is necessary, remember to do so smoothly, since a sudden power change can cause a skid.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.13, 'Shifting Gears'

question: A motorcycle has front and rear brakes. According to the handbook, how should they be used for a normal stop?
choice_a: Only the rear brake, for normal stops
choice_b: Only the front brake, for normal stops
choice_c: Both at the same time, every time you slow or stop
choice_d: Whichever brake is more convenient at the moment
explanation: Use both brakes every time you slow or stop, to develop the proper habit of using both brakes correctly in an emergency.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.13, 'Braking'

question: About how much of a motorcycle's total stopping power can the front brake provide, according to the handbook?
choice_b: None; the front brake is for steering assistance only
explanation: The front brake is more powerful and can provide at least three-quarters of your total stopping power, and is safe to use if used properly.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.13, 'Braking'

question: When applying the brakes, the correct technique is to:
choice_a: Squeeze the front brake lever and press down on the rear brake pedal
choice_b: Grab the front brake as hard and fast as possible
choice_c: Jam down on the rear brake pedal suddenly
choice_d: Only ever use the rear brake for any stop
explanation: Squeeze the front brake and press down on the rear. Grabbing at the front brake or jamming down on the rear can cause the brakes to lock, resulting in control problems.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.13, 'Braking'

question: When leaning a motorcycle through a turn, using the brakes:
choice_a: Has no relationship at all to available cornering traction
choice_b: Uses up traction that would otherwise be available for cornering, and can cause a skid if overapplied
choice_d: Is required at every turn regardless of conditions
explanation: When leaning the motorcycle, some traction is used for cornering, leaving less traction available for stopping; a skid can occur if you apply too much brake.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.13, 'Braking'

question: The four steps the handbook recommends for better control through a turn, in order, are:
explanation: Use four steps for better control in a turn: SLOW, LOOK, PRESS, ROLL.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.13, 'Turning'

question: During the "Look" step of turning, you should:
choice_a: Turn your head and shoulders together
choice_b: Keep your eyes fixed on the front wheel
choice_c: Close your eyes briefly to focus on the sensation of the turn
choice_d: Turn just your head, not your shoulders, keeping your eyes level with the horizon
explanation: LOOK -- Look through the turn to where you want to go, turning just your head, not your shoulders, and keeping your eyes level with the horizon.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.13, 'Turning'

question: During the "Press" step of turning, to turn the motorcycle you should:
choice_a: Press on the handgrip in the direction of the turn, causing the motorcycle to lean that way
choice_b: Pull back on both handgrips evenly
choice_c: Press on the handgrip opposite the direction of the turn
choice_d: Stand up on the footpegs before leaning
explanation: PRESS -- to turn, the motorcycle must lean. Press on the handgrip in the direction of the turn: press left, lean left, go left; press right, lean right, go right.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.13, 'Turning'

question: The "Roll" step of turning means you should:
choice_a: Roll off the throttle completely and coast through the turn
choice_b: Roll on the throttle through the turn to stabilize the suspension and maintain a steady speed
choice_c: Roll your shoulders to help counterbalance
choice_d: Apply the rear brake continuously through the turn
explanation: ROLL -- roll on the throttle through the turn to stabilize the suspension, maintaining a steady speed or accelerating gradually to help keep the motorcycle stable.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.13-14, 'Turning'

question: In slow, tight turns, the handbook recommends that riders counterbalance by:
choice_a: Leaning the body only, while keeping the motorcycle upright
choice_b: Leaning both the body and motorcycle sharply in the opposite direction
choice_c: Leaning the motorcycle only, while keeping the body straight
choice_d: Coming to a complete stop before turning
explanation: In slow, tight turns, counterbalance by leaning the motorcycle only and keeping your body straight.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.14, 'Turning'

question: In normal turns, how should the rider and motorcycle lean, according to the handbook?
choice_a: Only the motorcycle should lean; the rider should stay perfectly vertical
choice_b: Only the rider should lean; the motorcycle should stay perfectly vertical
choice_c: The rider should lean opposite to the motorcycle's lean angle
choice_d: The rider and motorcycle should lean together at the same angle
explanation: In normal turns, the rider and the motorcycle should lean together at the same angle.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.13, 'Turning'
